screens.title: Rank-nullity
screens.prose: **Rank-nullity** (Axler 3.21): for $T \in \mathcal{L}(V, W)$ with $V$ finite-dimensional, $$\dim V = \dim \ker T + \dim \operatorname{im} T.$$ $\dim \operatorname{im} T$ is the **rank** and $\dim \ker T$ the **nullity**. Take $T : \mathbb{R}^5 \to \mathbb{R}^3$, such as $\mathbf{x} \mapsto \mathbf{F}\mathbf{x}$.
screens.question: Can a linear $T : \mathbb{R}^5 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be injective?

options.text: Yes, if no column of its matrix is zero.
options.why: $\mathbf{F}$ has no zero column, yet five columns in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are dependent.

options.text: We cannot tell without the matrix.
options.why: The dimensions decide it: the image has dimension at most 3.

hints.text: The image sits inside $\mathbb{R}^3$.
So $\dim \operatorname{im} T \le 3$.
Then $\dim \ker T \ge 5 - 3 = 2 > 0$.

feedback.correct: Right. The kernel has dimension at least 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound the image, then use rank-nullity.

explain.text: The image lies in $\mathbb{R}^3$, so its dimension is at most 3. Rank-nullity leaves at least 2 for the kernel. A map into a space of smaller dimension is never injective.

screens.title: Step 2 of the proof
screens.prose: The proof. (1) Take a basis $(\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_m)$ of $\ker T$. (2) Extend it to a basis $(\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_m, \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n)$ of $V$. (3) Claim: $(T\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, T\mathbf{v}_n)$ is a basis of $\operatorname{im} T$. Then $\dim V = m + n$.
screens.question: Why can we extend $(\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_m)$ to a basis of $V$?

options.text: It is independent, and an independent list in a finite-dimensional space extends to a basis (l4, Axler 2.31).
Every list extends to a basis.
options.why: A dependent list such as $(\mathbf{e}_1, 2\mathbf{e}_1)$ lies in no basis.
It spans only $\ker T$. If it spanned $V$, there would be nothing to add.

options.text: $\ker T$ is a subspace, so its basis is already a basis of $V$.
options.why: Only when $\ker T = V$. For $D$, the basis $(1)$ of the constants is far from a basis of $\mathcal{P}_3$.

hints.text: What kind of list is a basis of $\ker T$, seen inside $V$?
It is independent in $V$.
l4: every independent list extends to a basis.

feedback.correct: Right. Independence is what the extension theorem needs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which property of the list does l4's extension theorem use?

explain.text: A basis of $\ker T$ is independent, and independence does not depend on the surrounding space. The extension theorem of l4 then adds $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$. For $D$ we may take $(1)$ and add $x, x^2, x^3$.

screens.title: Step 4: the images span
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $\mathbf{w} \in \operatorname{im} T$, so $\mathbf{w} = T\mathbf{v}$ for some $\mathbf{v} \in V$.
Write $\mathbf{v} = \sum a_i\mathbf{u}_i + \sum b_j\mathbf{v}_j$, as the list is a basis of $V$.
Then $\mathbf{w} = \sum a_iT\mathbf{u}_i + \sum b_jT\mathbf{v}_j$, by linearity.
Each $T\mathbf{u}_i = \mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{w} = \sum b_jT\mathbf{v}_j$.
So $(T\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, T\mathbf{v}_n)$ spans $\operatorname{im} T$.
Write $\mathbf{w} = \sum b_jT\mathbf{v}_j$, since each $T\mathbf{v}_j$ is in $\operatorname{im} T$.
lines.why: That assumes the spanning we are proving. Being in the image does not make the $T\mathbf{v}_j$ span it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand $\mathbf{v}$ in the full basis and apply $T$.

byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Every image vector is $T$ of a combination of the whole basis. The $\mathbf{u}_i$ terms vanish because they lie in the kernel. What is left is a combination of the $T\mathbf{v}_j$.

screens.title: Step 5: the images are independent
screens.prose: Show that $(T\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, T\mathbf{v}_n)$ is independent. Here the kernel basis earns its place.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $\sum c_jT\mathbf{v}_j = \mathbf{0}$.
Then $T(\sum c_j\mathbf{v}_j) = \mathbf{0}$, by linearity, so $\sum c_j\mathbf{v}_j \in \ker T$.
The $\mathbf{u}_i$ span $\ker T$, so $\sum c_j\mathbf{v}_j = \sum d_i\mathbf{u}_i$.
Then $\sum d_i\mathbf{u}_i - \sum c_j\mathbf{v}_j = \mathbf{0}$.
The whole list is a basis of $V$, so independent: every $c_j = 0$.
So $(T\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, T\mathbf{v}_n)$ is independent.
$T$ is injective, so $\sum c_j\mathbf{v}_j = \mathbf{0}$.
lines.why: $T$ need not be injective: $D$ is not. The combination lands in $\ker T$, not at $\mathbf{0}$.

hints.text: Pull the combination inside $T$.
It lies in $\ker T$, so write it with the $\mathbf{u}_i$.
Zero combination; kernel; write with $\mathbf{u}$s; rearrange; independence; conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. A zero combination of the $T\mathbf{v}_j$ forces every $c_j = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the basis of $\ker T$, then independence of the whole basis.

byKey.x1: You assumed $T$ is injective. The proof must work for every linear map, so route through $\ker T$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: The combination $\sum c_j\mathbf{v}_j$ lies in $\ker T$, so it is a combination of the $\mathbf{u}_i$. Moving everything to one side gives a zero combination of the full basis. Independence of that basis kills every $c_j$.

screens.title: The whole proof
screens.prose: Now assemble rank-nullity from its parts. This is the proof to know without notes.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $(\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_m)$ be a basis of $\ker T$, so $\dim \ker T = m$.
Extend it by $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ to a basis of $V$ (Axler 2.31), so $\dim V = m + n$.
Claim: $(T\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, T\mathbf{v}_n)$ is a basis of $\operatorname{im} T$.
It spans: $T(\sum a_i\mathbf{u}_i + \sum b_j\mathbf{v}_j) = \sum b_jT\mathbf{v}_j$, as each $T\mathbf{u}_i = \mathbf{0}$.
It is independent: $\sum c_jT\mathbf{v}_j = \mathbf{0}$ puts $\sum c_j\mathbf{v}_j$ in $\ker T$.
So $\sum c_j\mathbf{v}_j = \sum d_i\mathbf{u}_i$, and independence of the basis of $V$ gives every $c_j = 0$.
So $\dim \operatorname{im} T = n$.
Hence $\dim V = m + n = \dim \ker T + \dim \operatorname{im} T$. $\blacksquare$
Each $T\mathbf{v}_j \ne \mathbf{0}$, so the $T\mathbf{v}_j$ are independent.
lines.why: Non-zero vectors can be dependent: $(1, 0)$ and $(2, 0)$. Independence needs the kernel argument.

State the claim, then prove spanning and independence.
Kernel basis; extend; claim; spans; independent (two lines); count; conclude.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the bases first, then prove the claim, then count.

explain.text: The kernel basis has $m$ vectors and the extension adds $n$ more. Their images under $T$ are a basis of the image, so the rank is $n$. Adding gives $m + n = \dim V$.

screens.title: Counting solutions
screens.prose: If $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_p = \mathbf{b}$, every solution of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is $\mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{k}$ with $\mathbf{k} \in \ker \mathbf{A}$. If $\mathbf{b} \notin \operatorname{im} \mathbf{A}$, there are none. $\mathbf{F}$ has rank 3, so $\operatorname{im} \mathbf{F} = \mathbb{R}^3$.
screens.question: For each $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^3$, the solutions of $\mathbf{F}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ form $\mathbf{x}_p + \ker \mathbf{F}$. What is $\dim \ker \mathbf{F}$?

hints.text: $\mathbf{F}$ maps $\mathbb{R}^5$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Rank-nullity: $5 = \dim \ker \mathbf{F} + 3$.
$\dim \ker \mathbf{F} = 5 - 3 = 2$.

feedback.correct: Right. $5 - 3 = 2$: a plane of solutions for every $\mathbf{b}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the rank from the number of columns.

byKey.rank: You gave the rank. The kernel takes what is left of the 5 inputs.
byKey.cols: You counted all inputs. Three dimensions go into the image.
byKey.rows: You used rows minus rank. The kernel lives among the 5 columns' inputs.

explain.text: The first three columns are independent, so the rank is 3 and every $\mathbf{b}$ is reached. Rank-nullity gives a kernel of dimension $5 - 3 = 2$. So each $\mathbf{b}$ has a two-dimensional family of solutions.

screens.title: Rows or columns?
screens.prose: $\mathbf{B}$ is $3 \times 5$. Its third row is the sum of the first two, so its rank is 2. A classmate computes the nullity as rows minus rank.
screens.question: What is the nullity of $\mathbf{B}$?

hints.text: The kernel holds inputs. How many entries does an input have?
$\mathbf{B}$ maps $\mathbb{R}^5$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$, so $\dim V = 5$.
Nullity $= 5 - 2 = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rank-nullity counts the domain, which has one dimension per column.

byKey.mr: You used rows minus rank, $3 - 2$. The domain is $\mathbb{R}^5$: subtract the rank from the 5 columns.
byKey.nm: You used columns minus rows, as if the rank were 3. Row 3 is row 1 plus row 2, so the rank is 2.

explain.text: $R_3 = R_1 + R_2$, so only two rows are independent and the rank is 2. The domain is $\mathbb{R}^5$, so the nullity is $5 - 2 = 3$. Rows minus rank counts something else: the left null space of `least-squares` l2.

screens.title: Rank-nullity in code
screens.prose: The starter computes the nullity as rows minus rank, the trap we just met. Fix it. Then return a kernel basis from the SVD $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^T$: the rows of $\mathbf{V}^T$ beyond the rank span $\ker \mathbf{A}$.

`np.linalg.svd(A)` returns `U, s, Vt`, with `Vt` of size $n \times n$.
Return `Vt[r:].T`, the last $n - r$ rows of `Vt` as columns.

feedback.correct: Right. Columns minus rank, and the SVD's last rows span the kernel.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row: is it the nullity or the kernel's shape?

byKey.test-1: Check the nullity: $\mathbf{B}$ has 5 columns and rank 2, so 3.
byKey.test-5: The identity has a zero kernel: return an $n \times 0$ array, which `Vt[n:].T` gives.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Does `kernel_basis` still return `None`?

explain.text:
The kernel has dimension $n - r$, counted along the columns. The SVD's rows of $\mathbf{V}^T$ past the rank are orthonormal and sent to $\mathbf{0}$. So they form a basis of $\ker \mathbf{A}$.

```python
_, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
return Vt[r:].T
```

screens.title: More neutral portfolios than planned
screens.prose: Five stocks have exposures to three factors, one row per factor. A portfolio is factor-neutral when all three exposures are 0: it lies in the kernel. Last year's exposures were $\mathbf{F}$, with 2 neutral directions. This year's are $\mathbf{B}$, where one factor is the sum of the other two.
screens.question: What does rank-nullity tell the desk about this year?

options.text: The rank fell to 2, so there are $5 - 2 = 3$ independent neutral portfolios.

options.why: The shape does not fix the nullity. The rank fell, so the kernel grew.

options.text: 1: three factors minus a rank of 2.
options.why: You subtracted from the rows. The kernel lives among the 5 stocks.

options.text: None: dependent factors break the hedge.
options.why: Dependence enlarges the kernel. There are more neutral portfolios, not fewer.

hints.text: Find the rank of this year's matrix.
Row 3 is row 1 plus row 2, so the rank is 2.
Nullity $= 5 - 2 = 3$, one more than last year.

feedback.correct: Right. One factor is redundant, so a third neutral direction appears.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute this year's rank, then subtract it from the 5 stocks.

explain.text: With $\mathbf{F}$, rank 3 leaves $5 - 3 = 2$ neutral directions. With $\mathbf{B}$, a redundant factor cuts the rank to 2, so $5 - 2 = 3$. Any portfolio neutral to two of the factors is now neutral to the third for free.

ideas: Rank-nullity: $\dim V = \dim \ker T + \dim \operatorname{im} T$. Each input dimension dies in the kernel or survives into the image.
The proof extends a basis of $\ker T$ to a basis of $V$. The images of the added vectors form a basis of the image.
Solutions of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ are $\mathbf{x}_p + \ker \mathbf{A}$ when $\mathbf{b} \in \operatorname{im} \mathbf{A}$, and there are none otherwise.
